subject: Biology
title: The Nitrogen Cycle
description: Learn The Nitrogen Cycle in one minute.

hook.text: Nitrogen makes up 78% of the air, but most organisms can't use it directly.

buildup.text: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert N₂ gas into ammonia that plants can absorb through roots.

discovery.text: Animals get nitrogen by eating plants. When things die, decomposers return nitrogen to the soil.

twist.text: Synthetic fertilizers flood ecosystems with excess nitrogen, causing algae blooms and dead zones.

climax.text: The Gulf of Mexico's dead zone—caused by fertilizer runoff—covers thousands of square kilometers.

punchline.text: Too little nitrogen starves. Too much kills.

quiz.question: Why can't most organisms use atmospheric nitrogen directly?
options: It must be converted by bacteria first
It only exists in the upper atmosphere

details.summary: The nitrogen cycle converts atmospheric nitrogen into forms organisms can use. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert N2 into ammonia, which plants absorb. Animals obtain nitrogen by eating plants, and decomposers return it to soil. Denitrifying bacteria release N2 back to the atmosphere.
details.whyItMatters: Nitrogen is essential for proteins and DNA but atmospheric N2 is unusable by most organisms. Human fertilizer production has doubled reactive nitrogen in the biosphere, causing water pollution, dead zones, and greenhouse gas emissions.
takeaways: Only nitrogen-fixing bacteria can convert atmospheric N2 into usable forms
Human fertilizer production has doubled the amount of reactive nitrogen globally
Excess nitrogen causes algal blooms and aquatic dead zones

faq.question: Why cannot most organisms use atmospheric nitrogen?
faq.answer: Atmospheric N2 has an extremely strong triple bond between its two atoms. Only specialized nitrogen-fixing bacteria possess the nitrogenase enzyme powerful enough to break this bond and convert N2 into ammonia that living organisms can incorporate.

faq.question: How does excess nitrogen cause dead zones?
faq.answer: Fertilizer runoff carries nitrogen into waterways, fueling explosive algal growth. When the algae die, decomposing bacteria consume all available oxygen, creating hypoxic zones where fish and other marine life suffocate. The Gulf of Mexico dead zone exceeds 15,000 square kilometers.
